notes.statement: Burbulla et al. (2017) found that iPSC-derived dopaminergic neurons from 2 patients with idiopathic PD showed decreased basal mitochondrial respiration and accumulated oxidized dopamine, and later had decreased lysosomal glucocerebrosidase (GCase) activity. These changes appeared at later time points (day 150-180) than in neurons with homozygous DJ-1 mutations. Partial inactivation of DJ-1 was seen in the idiopathic PD neurons, which suggested that decreased DJ-1 function might contribute.
quotes: Dopaminergic neurons from idiopathic PD patients (iPD1,; iPD2, fig. S1, E and F) also manifested a similar phenotype, including decreased basal respiration and oxidized dopamine accumulation, but at later time points (d150, d180)
We observed partial inactivation of DJ-1 in iPD neurons (fig. S4B), suggesting that decreased DJ-1 function may contribute to these delayed pathological alterations in iPD neurons.
Idiopathic PD neurons exhibited a delayed decrease in GCase activity (d180) compared to DJ-1 mutant neurons (d70)

notes.statement: Burbulla et al. (2017) proposed a time-dependent pathologic cascade in human PD dopaminergic neurons. In this cascade, mitochondrial oxidant stress led to accumulation of oxidized dopamine. Dopamine quinones modified cysteine residues in the GCase catalytic site and reduced its activity, which caused lysosomal dysfunction and alpha-synuclein accumulation. Similar increases in oxidized dopamine were seen in neurons from patients with parkin, PINK1, or LRRK2 mutations and with alpha-synuclein triplication, which suggested a mechanism common to sporadic and familial PD.
quotes: We identified a time-dependent pathological cascade beginning with mitochondrial oxidant stress leading to oxidized dopamine accumulation and ultimately resulting in reduced glucocerebrosidase enzymatic activity, lysosomal dysfunction, and α-synuclein accumulation.
Using tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS), we identified cysteine residues in the catalytic site of GCase that were modified by dopamine quinones, reactive oxidized forms of dopamine

We observed a similar increase in oxidized dopamine across all genotypes (fig. S4C, E to G) as well as decreased GCase activity in parkin mutant neurons (fig. S4D), further suggesting the presence of common phenotypes across both sporadic and familial forms of PD.

notes.statement: Burbulla et al. (2017) found that DJ-1 knockout mice did not show the toxic cascade seen in human neurons. They had little oxidized dopamine and no nigral neuron loss. However, overexpressing human A53T alpha-synuclein or chronically feeding L-DOPA to DJ-1 knockout mice increased oxidized dopamine and reduced GCase activity, and L-DOPA also caused loss of dopaminergic neurons. The authors attributed the species difference partly to higher dopamine levels and calcineurin activity in human neurons.
quotes: In contrast to human neurons, SNc from DJ-1 KO mice showed negligible amounts of oxidized dopamine at 3 and 12 months of age

L-DOPA treatment in DJ-1 KO mice but not in WT mice was sufficient to disrupt SNc GCase enzymatic activity (Fig. 4G), increase α-synuclein accumulation (Fig. 4H, fig. S7D), and trigger the loss of dopaminergic neurons
Control human neurons showed both increased protein levels and activity of calcineurin (Fig. 5, D and E) compared to mouse WT neurons

notes.statement: In DJ-1 mutant human dopaminergic neurons, Burbulla et al. (2017) found that long-term treatment with the antioxidants mito-TEMPO or N-acetyl cysteine reduced oxidized dopamine accumulation and improved lysosomal function. Treatment with isradipine or FK506 also reduced oxidized dopamine. The authors concluded that early therapeutic intervention in the cascade was important.
quotes: We found that long-term treatment with either the mitochondrial-targeted antioxidant mito-TEMPO or NAC blunted the accumulation of oxidized dopamine and improved lysosomal GCase activity and proteolysis
Both isradipine and FK506 significantly diminished the accumulation of oxidized dopamine

notes.statement: Mittal et al. (2017) screened 1,126 compounds for their effect on endogenous SNCA expression in human SK-N-MC neuroblastoma cells. Three of the 4 confirmed hits were beta-2-adrenoreceptor (beta2AR) agonists (metaproterenol, clenbuterol and salbutamol), and these lowered SNCA mRNA and alpha-synuclein protein in a dose- and time-dependent manner. The agonists also reduced SNCA mRNA and protein in rat primary cortical neurons.
quotes: We screened 1126 compounds, including drugs approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and a diverse set of natural products, vitamins, health supplements, and alkaloids (data S1 and fig. S1).
Unexpectedly, three of these hits were β2AR agonists (Fig. 1B), and these were prioritized for further investigation.
β2AR agonists lowered SNCA expression in a dose- and time-dependent manner (fig. S5).

notes.statement: Mittal et al. (2017) found that beta2AR modulation regulated SNCA expression in both directions. Knockout of Adrb2 in mouse neurons, silencing of beta2AR, or treatment with propranolol increased SNCA mRNA and protein, whereas overexpressing ADRB2 lowered SNCA. Beta2AR regulated SNCA transcription through H3K27 acetylation at the SNCA promoter and 2 intronic enhancers: clenbuterol reduced H3K27ac and propranolol increased it.
quotes: Endogenous Snca mRNA and α-synuclein protein levels were increased by 100 and 120%, respectively, compared with those in controls (P = 0.004 and 0.01, respectively; Student’s t test) (Fig. 2, E and F).

Clenbuterol treatment reduced H3K27ac across the promoter (site 1, Fig. 3A) and two putative intronic enhancers (sites 2 and 3, Fig. 3A), compared with vehicle treatment (P < 0.05; one-way ANOVA with Tukey’s).
Thus, β2AR regulates the transcription of α-synuclein in correlation with H3K27ac across the promoter and enhancers in the human SNCA locus.

notes.statement: Mittal et al. (2017) followed the entire Norwegian population (4.6 million people) for 11 years. Use of the beta2AR agonist salbutamol was associated with a reduced risk of PD (rate ratio 0.66; 95% CI, 0.58-0.76), with a dose-response relationship. Use of the beta2AR antagonist propranolol was associated with an increased risk (rate ratio 2.20; 95% CI, 1.62-3.00). The authors noted that association does not imply causation.
quotes: Salbutamol was associated with decreased risk of PD, with a rate ratio of 0.66 [95% confidence interval (CI), 0.58 to 0.76] (Tables 1 and 2, Fig. 4A, and fig. S9). Propranolol was associated with a markedly increased risk of PD, with a rate ratio of 2.20 (95% CI, 1.62 to 3.00) (Table 1 and Fig. 4B).
It is important to note that association does not imply causation.

notes.statement: Mittal et al. (2017) found that clenbuterol crossed the blood-brain barrier and lowered alpha-synuclein mRNA and protein in the substantia nigra of wildtype mice. In MPTP-treated mice, clenbuterol prevented the loss of tyrosine hydroxylase-positive neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta.
quotes: β2AR activation lowered the expression of endogenous α-synuclein protein and mRNA levels in the PD vulnerable substantia nigra (P = 0.01; two-tailed Student’s t test) (Fig. 2D).
Clenbuterol treatment abrogated the MPTP-induced loss of TH+ neurons (Fig. 4, C and D) and, importantly, also blocked the loss of cresyl violet–stained cells in the SNpc (Fig. 4E and fig. S10).

notes.statement: Mittal et al. (2017) studied iPSC-derived neuronal precursor cells from a patient with PD due to SNCA triplication. Clenbuterol reduced SNCA mRNA and protein in these cells, lowered mitochondria-associated superoxide production, and increased their viability when exposed to rotenone. The authors proposed that beta2AR antagonists increase SNCA expression through H3K27 acetylation and thereby increase PD risk.
quotes: SNCA-triplication iPSC-derived neuronal precursor cells were treated with clenbuterol (20 μM), and endogenous SNCA mRNA expression and α-synuclein protein levels were significantly reduced (P < 0.005 and 0.05, respectively; two-tailed Student’s t test) (Fig. 4F).
Clenbuterol treatment ameliorated this increased mitochondria-associated superoxide production (Fig. 4G) and increased viability (Fig. 4H), similarly to partial SNCA knockdown.

We propose a model in which β2AR antagonists increase SNCA expression through H3K27 acetylation, resulting in α-synuclein accumulation, mitochondrial oxidative stress, dopaminergic neurodegeneration, and increased risk of PD.

notes.statement: Sulzer et al. (2017) studied 67 PD patients and 36 age-matched healthy controls. About one-third of the PD patients carried the HLA class II alleles DRB1*15:01/DRB5*01:01, compared with about 15% of controls (p = 0.036 and 0.022).
quotes: we recruited 67 PD participants and 36 age-matched non-PD healthy controls (HC)
While ~15% of HC carried DRB1*15:01/DRB5*01:01 alleles, ~1/3 of PD carried these alleles (difference between PD and HC, p=0.036 and 0.022 for DRB1*15:01/DRB5*01:01)

notes.statement: Sulzer et al. (2017) found that PBMCs from PD patients responded to 2 antigenic regions of alpha-synuclein. The first was near the N terminus (the Y39 region, aa31-46). The second was near the C terminus (aa116-140) and required phosphorylation of S129. Responses were mainly IL-5-secreting CD4+ T cells, with some IFN-gamma-producing CD8+ T cells, and were significantly greater in PD patients than in controls.
quotes: We identified two antigenic regions in α-syn, the first near the N terminus, composed of aa31GKTKEGVLYVGSKTK aa45 and aa32KTKEGVLYVGSKTKE aa46 (referred to as the Y39 region)
The second antigenic region was near the C terminus (aa116–140) (referred to as the S129 region) (Fig 1a), and required phosphorylation of amino acid residue S129.
The response was primarily polarized towards IL-5 in PD (71% IL-5 and 29% IFNγ; Fig. 2d).

notes.statement: Sulzer et al. (2017) showed that the Y39-region epitope bound the PD-associated alleles DRB1*15:01 and DRB5*01:01 with high affinity (2.8 nM and 8.1 nM). Among PD patients, 8 of 13 responders to this epitope carried both alleles. Together, DRB1*15:01, DRB5*01:01, DQB1*03:04, and the class I allele A*11:01 accounted for every PD patient who responded to the Y39 epitope (p = 0.00007).
quotes: The HLA class II variants DRB1*15:01 and DRB5*01:01 bound the epitope with high affinity (2.8 nM and 8.1 nM, respectively)

Of PD participants, 8/13 responders to the aa32KTKEGVLYVGSKTKEaa46 epitope expressed both DRB1*15:01 and DRB5*01:01, while only 12/45 (DRB1*15:01) and 13/43 (DRB5*01:01) non-responders expressed the alleles
The four alleles DRB1*15:01, DRB5*01:01, DQB1*03:04 and A*11:01 accounted for every single individual responding to the aa39 epitope (p=0.00007 for PD, Table 1).

notes.statement: Sulzer et al. (2017) found that about 40% of the PD patients had immune responses to alpha-synuclein epitopes. T-cell lines specific for these epitopes were activated by antigen-presenting cells pulsed with native or fibrillized alpha-synuclein. The authors suggested that these responses may explain the association of PD with specific MHC alleles.
quotes: Approximately 40% of the PD participants in our cohort exhibited immune responses to α-syn epitopes
T cells lines specific for the α-syn epitopes were activated by antigen presenting cells pulsed with native or PFF protein in 7/12 and 11/12 cases.
These responses may explain the association of Parkinson's disease with specific major histocompatibility complex alleles.

notes.statement: Sulzer et al. (2017) found that the 9-mer alpha-synuclein peptide aa37-45 (VLYVGSKTK) bound HLA-A*11:01 (IC50 = 161 nM). Five of 19 PD patients, and none of 12 controls, responded to short class I candidate peptides. The authors concluded that PD-associated immune responses to alpha-synuclein have both MHC class I- and class II-restricted components.
quotes: We found that 5/19 PD responded to these short peptides while 0/12 HC responded
the 9mer aa37VLYVGSKTKaa45, which is nested within the two 10mers, bound with good affinity (IC50 = 161 nM)
Thus, immune responses to α-syn associated with PD have both MHC class I and II restricted components.

notes.statement: Tell-Marti et al. (2015) sequenced the entire MC1R gene in 870 Parkinson disease patients and 736 controls from Spain. The MC1R p.R160W variant (rs1805008) was marginally associated with PD (odds ratio = 2.10; gender- and age-adjusted p = 0.009; Bonferroni-corrected p = 0.063). The authors suggested that MC1R genetic variants modulate the risk of PD in the Spanish population.
quotes: sequencing the entire gene in 870 PD patients and 736 controls ascertained from Spain
We found that the MC1R variant p.R160W (rs1805008) is marginally associated with PD (odds ratio = 2.10, gender- and age-adjusted p = 0.009, Bonferroni-corrected p = 0.063).
Our results suggest that MC1R genetic variants modulate the risk of PD disease in the Spanish population.

notes.statement: Tell-Marti et al. (2015) noted that epidemiologic studies had reported that Parkinson disease and melanoma occur together. Common MC1R variants, which determine skin and hair color, are associated with melanoma.
quotes: Epidemiological studies have reported the co-occurrence of Parkinson disease (PD) and melanoma.
Common genetic variants in the MC1R (melanocortin 1 receptor) gene, which determines skin and hair color, are associated with melanoma.

notes.statement: In an expression QTL study of purified CD4+ T cells and CD14+CD16- monocytes from 461 healthy individuals of European, African, and East Asian ancestry, Raj et al. (2014) found that susceptibility alleles for Parkinson disease and Alzheimer disease were enriched for monocyte-specific cis-eQTL effects. By contrast, susceptibility alleles for autoimmune diseases such as multiple sclerosis and rheumatoid arthritis were enriched for T cell-specific effects.
quotes: We note an over-representation of T cell-specific eQTLs among susceptibility alleles for autoimmune diseases and of monocyte-specific eQTLs among Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease variants.

Four diseases with significant polarization (FDR < 0.05) in the distribution of cis-eQTLs: Multiple sclerosis and rheumatoid arthritis are enriched in T cell effects (green), whereas Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s diseases are enriched in monocyte effects (orange).

notes.statement: Raj et al. (2014) suggested that the inflammatory component of susceptibility to neurodegenerative diseases such as PD may be driven more strongly by the myeloid compartment of the immune system. They proposed that blood monocytes may act as proxies for infiltrating macrophages and/or resident microglia at sites of neuropathology.
quotes: we suggest that the inflammatory component of susceptibility to neurodegenerative diseases may be more strongly driven by the myeloid compartment of the immune system.
they are likely to be proxies for the infiltrating macrophages (which differentiate from monocytes) and/or resident microglia found at the sites of neuropathology.

notes.statement: In the PAGE study (808 PD cases and 1,623 controls, all non-Hispanic white), Dong et al. (2014) tested 11 SNPs that earlier GWAS had linked to pigmentation or melanoma. After Bonferroni correction, none was associated with PD risk except rs4911414 at the ASIP gene (p = 0.001). In the larger IPDGC dataset (5,333 cases and 12,019 controls), rs4911414 was not associated with PD (P = 0.43), and none of the 360 pigmentation or melanoma SNPs tested reached significance.
quotes: neither these SNPs nor pigmentation phenotypes were associated with PD risk after Bonferroni correction with the exception of rs4911414 at the ASIP gene (p = .001)

However, this SNP was not associated with PD risk in the larger dataset of IPDGC (P=0.43), and none of the other 359 SNPs selected for analysis in the IPDGC dataset showed statistical significance with PD

notes.statement: Dong et al. (2014) found that MC1R rs1805007, a SNP a previous study had associated with PD, was not significantly associated with PD in the IPDGC dataset (OR 1.06, 95% CI 0.94-1.19, P = 0.37). The authors noted that they did not study high-penetrance melanoma genes such as CDKN2 and CDK4, so they could not exclude a role for other genes in the melanoma-PD link.
quotes: In the IPDGC, rs1805007 at MC1R, the SNP that showed significant association with PD in the previous study had an OR of 1.06 (95%CI: 0.94-1.19, P=0.37).
Thus, we cannot exclude the possibility that other genes may explain the association between melanoma and PD.

notes.statement: In the PAGE study, Dong et al. (2014) found a diagnosis of melanoma in 18 PD cases (2.2%) and 26 controls (1.6%). This gave a modest but nonsignificant positive association (OR 1.32, 95% CI 0.71-2.44). Hair, eye and skin color were not associated with PD risk.
quotes: A total of 18 PD cases (2.2%) and 26 controls (1.6%) had a diagnosis of melanoma with an odds ratio of 1.3 (95% confidence interval: 0.7-2.4).
In the PAGE study, neither pigmentation phenotypes nor melanoma were statistically associated with PD risk.

notes.statement: In a phenotypic screen of yeast expressing toxic levels of alpha-synuclein, Tardiff et al. (2013) identified an N-aryl benzimidazole (NAB) that reversed the alpha-synuclein phenotypes: vesicular alpha-synuclein foci, reactive oxygen species, the ER-to-Golgi trafficking block, and protein nitration. NAB did this without lowering alpha-synuclein levels.
quotes: NAB reversed diverse phenotypes caused by α–syn, including the accumulation of vesicular α-syn foci (Fig. 1C), the generation of reactive oxygen species (Fig. 1D), the block of ER-Golgi trafficking (Fig. 1E), and the nitration of proteins.
NAB did not reduce α-syn accumulation (Fig. 1E).

notes.statement: Tardiff et al. (2013) found that NAB reversed alpha-synuclein toxicity or pathology in three neuronal systems: C. elegans dopaminergic neurons, rat primary midbrain cultures expressing A53T alpha-synuclein, and cortical neurons derived from induced pluripotent stem cells of PD patients carrying the A53T mutation or an alpha-synuclein triplication. The authors suggested that NAB marks a 'druggable' node in alpha-synuclein biology.
quotes: Third, we tested cortical neurons differentiated from PD-patient induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) carrying either the A53T α–syn mutation or an α-syn triplication, both of which caused protein trafficking defects and nitrosative stress.
In each case, NAB reversed α–syn toxicity or pathology, suggesting the compound’s target and mechanisms of action (MOA) were conserved from yeast to human cells

notes.statement: Tardiff et al. (2013) used chemical genetic screens in yeast to show that NAB acts through the E3 ubiquitin ligase Rsp5 (the yeast homolog of NEDD4) to promote endosomal transport. A point mutation, rsp5 G747E, made cells resistant to NAB. Alpha-synuclein itself impaired Rsp5-dependent endosomal trafficking of Mup1 and Sna3 and bulk endocytosis, and NAB2 restored these processes.
quotes: Three chemical genetic screens in wild-type yeast cells established that NAB promoted endosomal transport events dependent on the E3 ubiquitin ligase Rsp5/Nedd4. These same steps were perturbed by α-syn itself.

Indeed, α–syn expression impeded both the methionine-induced transport of Mup1-GFP from the plasma membrane to the vacuole (Fig. 4A) and the constitutive trafficking of Sna3-GFP from the Golgi and the vacuole (Fig. 4B).
Together, these analyses established Rsp5 as the central node and only potential protein target within the NAB network.

notes.statement: Chung et al. (2013) generated cortical neurons from iPS cells of a Contursi kindred patient with the SNCA A53T mutation and mutation-corrected isogenic controls. A53T neurons showed increased nitric oxide and nitrotyrosine, early and progressive accumulation of ER forms of the ERAD substrates glucocerebrosidase and nicastrin, and increased ER stress markers PDI and BIP, without change in CHOP; neurons from an SNCA triplication patient closely phenocopied these defects.
quotes: Intraneuronal FL2 signals increased in A53T neurons relative to corrected neurons, again most readily visualized in the cell body.
ER forms of GCase and Nicastrin accumulated, and the ratio of post ER/ER forms declined in A53T compared to mutation-corrected patient neurons starting at four weeks
ERAD substrates accumulated (fig. 3A and fig. S6B) and ER stress increased (fig. S5C) in neurons from this patient, closely phenocopying A53T cells.

notes.statement: In a yeast alpha-synuclein toxicity model, Chung et al. (2013) found that protein nitration was a specific, dosage-dependent response to alpha-synuclein, and that increasing or decreasing nitric oxide production commensurately altered toxicity, indicating that nitrosative stress contributes to rather than merely results from alpha-synuclein toxicity.
quotes: nitration was a highly specific response to αSyn toxicity and was not observed with other neurodegenerative disease proteins expressed at equally toxic levels
Thus, in yeast, nitrosative stress is not simply a consequence of αSyn toxicity, but contributes to toxicity.

notes.statement: Chung et al. (2013) found that the small molecule NAB2, identified in a yeast screen and acting via the Rsp5/Nedd4 ubiquitin ligase pathway, decreased nitric oxide levels and corrected ER accumulation of nicastrin and glucocerebrosidase in A53T patient neurons; lentiviral Nedd4 overexpression phenocopied NAB2, and the ERAD E3 ligase synoviolin (SYVN1) also reduced ER accumulation of these substrates and rescued alpha-synuclein toxicity in rat cortical neurons.
quotes: NAB2 reduced protein nitration in the yeast syucleinopathy model (fig. 4A) and decreased NO levels in A53T patient neurons (fig. 4B).
Connecting NAB2 back to the ubiquitin ligase, we used a lentivirus to overexpress Nedd4. This phenocopied the effects of the compound, increasing the mature forms of Nicastrin and GCase (fig. 4D).
Syvn1 also reduced nicastrin and GCase accumulation in the ER of the A53T patient cortical neurons (fig. 3E).

notes.statement: Chung et al. (2013) noted that cortex from sporadic PD samples showed the same trend toward increased ER forms of glucocerebrosidase as seen in A53T patient brain.
quotes: Cortex from sporadic PD samples exhibited the same trend (fig. S7).

notes.statement: Miñones-Moyano et al. (2011) found decreased expression of miR-34b and miR-34c in PD brain areas with variable neuropathologic involvement, including the amygdala, frontal cortex, substantia nigra, and cerebellum, at clinical motor stages (Braak stages 4 and 5). Misregulation of miR-34b/c was also detected at premotor stages (Braak stages 1-3), in cases that had not received PD-related treatment.
quotes: MiRNA expression profiling revealed decreased expression of miR-34b and miR-34c in brain areas with variable neuropathological affectation at clinical (motor) stages (Braak stages 4 and 5) of the disease, including the amygdala, frontal cortex, substantia nigra and cerebellum.
misregulation of miR-34b/c was detected in pre-motor stages (stages 1-3) of the disease, and thus in cases that did not receive any PD-related treatment during life.

notes.statement: Miñones-Moyano et al. (2011) found that depleting miR-34b or miR-34c in differentiated SH-SY5Y dopaminergic neuronal cells moderately reduced cell viability. This was accompanied by altered mitochondrial function and dynamics, oxidative stress, reduced cellular ATP, and decreased expression of DJ1 and Parkin. DJ1 and Parkin expression was also reduced in PD brain samples with strong miR-34b/c downregulation. The authors proposed that early deregulation of miR-34b/c in PD triggers downstream transcriptome changes that underlie mitochondrial dysfunction and oxidative stress.
quotes: Depletion of miR-34b or miR-34c in differentiated SH-SY5Y dopaminergic neuronal cells resulted in a moderate reduction in cell viability that was accompanied by altered mitochondrial function and dynamics, oxidative stress and reduction in total cellular adenosin triphosphate content.
MiR-34b/c downregulation was coupled to a decrease in the expression of DJ1 and Parkin
Accordingly, DJ1 and Parkin expression was reduced in PD brain samples displaying strong miR-34b/c downregulation.

notes.statement: Berman et al. (2011) found that EAAC1 (SLC1A1)-null mice, which have impaired neuronal cysteine uptake and reduced neuronal glutathione, showed age-dependent loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta, with no difference at 3 months but a 41% decrease by 12 months. The neuronal loss was accompanied by increased nitrotyrosine formation, nitrosylated alpha-synuclein (mainly dimers and higher-order aggregates), and microglial activation.
quotes: EAAC1(-/-) mice showed age-dependent loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta, with more than 40% of these neurons lost by age 12 months. This neuronal loss was accompanied by increased nitrotyrosine formation, nitrosylated α-synuclein, and microglial activation.
No differences were found at 3 months, but a significant, 41 ± 10% decrease in the EAAC1−/− brains was apparent by age 12 months (see Fig 1).

notes.statement: Berman et al. (2011) found that striatal dopamine levels were only nonsignificantly reduced in EAAC1-null mice, and motor deficits were seen only on the pole test at 12 months. The authors concluded that the mouse models the chronic neuronal oxidative stress of PD but not its motor deficits.
quotes: Despite these changes in the SNc, measurements of dopamine and related biogenic amines in the striatum showed only nonsignificant reductions in the EAAC1−/−mice (Supporting Information Fig S3).
The EAAC1−/− mouse does not, however, provide a good model of the motor deficits in PD; deficits were found only with the pole test, and only at 12 months of age.

notes.statement: Berman et al. (2011) found that oral N-acetylcysteine, a membrane-permeable cysteine prodrug, restored reactive thiol content in nigral dopaminergic neurons of EAAC1-null mice. Long-term treatment from weaning to 12 months reduced dopaminergic neuron loss, nitrotyrosine immunoreactivity, and pole test deficits. The authors suggested that these results support clinical evaluation of glutathione repletion in PD.
quotes: Dopaminergic neurons from the EAAC1−/− mice showed significantly less C5-maleimide staining than neurons from WT mice, and this reduction was reversed in EAAC1−/− mice fed NAC (Fig 5).
A key finding here is that long-term oral administration of NAC prevents the neuronal death, oxidative stress, and motor abnormalities otherwise observed in the aged EAAC1−/− mice.
The salutary effects of N-acetylcysteine in this mouse model provide an impetus for clinical evaluation of glutathione repletion in PD.

notes.statement: Berman et al. (2011) found that EAAC1 expression was higher on tyrosine hydroxylase-positive dopaminergic neurons than on other neurons in both mouse and normal human midbrain. Surviving dopaminergic neurons in postmortem PD brains also expressed EAAC1. The authors suggested that EAAC1 plays a key role in dopaminergic neuronal glutathione metabolism.
quotes: As in the mouse brain, normal human brain showed increased EAAC1 expression in dopaminergic (TH-positive) neurons (see Fig 4B).
The TH-positive dopaminergic neurons show coexpression of EAAC1 in both PD and control brains.
Together, these findings suggest a key role for EAAC1 in dopaminergic neuronal glutathione metabolism and a contributory role for glutathione depletion in dopaminergic neuronal death.

notes.statement: Mata et al. (2011) genotyped SNPs in 1,445 Parkinson disease patients and 1,161 controls from northern Spain. They found significant association with SNPs in MAPT (rs1800547; OR 0.79, p = 3.1 x 10(-4)) and SNCA (rs356219; OR 1.23, p = 5.5 x 10(-4)). In analyses stratified by age, the association was significant only in the late-onset group.
quotes: We genotyped single-nucleotide polymorphisms in each of these genes/loci in 1445 Parkinson's disease patients and 1161 controls from northern Spain.

there was a highly significant association between PD and SNPs in MAPT (rs1800547; odds ratio [OR], 0.79; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.70–0.90; p = 3.1 × 10−4) and SNCA (rs356219; OR, 1.23; 95% CI, 1.09–1.38; p = 5.5 × 10−4)
In the age-stratified analyses, a significant association with PD was seen only for MAPT and SNCA in the late-onset group (Supplemental Table 1).

notes.statement: Mata et al. (2011) found that the A allele of MAPT rs1800547, a surrogate marker for the H1 haplotype, was associated with Parkinson disease under a dominant model (OR 1.23, p = 1.1 x 10(-2)) in their Spanish sample.
quotes: The “A” allele of rs1800547 serves as a surrogate marker for the MAPT “H1” haplotype
In our dataset, analysis of the A allele in an adjusted dominant model yielded an OR of 1.23 (95% CI, 1.05–1.44; p = 1.1 × 10−2).

notes.statement: Mata et al. (2011) found no association with Parkinson disease for SNPs at PARK16 (rs823156, rs947211), PARK17 (GAK rs11248051) or PARK18 (HLA-DRA rs3129882) in their Spanish case-control sample, overall or in any age stratum, with p values from 0.09 to 0.88. For PARK18 the study had 99% power at the originally reported OR. The authors suggested that population structure, power, or population-specific environmental interactions might explain the discordance, and that these loci needed further validation.
quotes: However, none of the markers in PARK16-18 associated with Parkinson's disease in the overall sample, or in any age stratum, with P values ranging from .09 to .88.
In contrast, we failed to detect an association of this SNP with PD in our sample (OR, 1.01; p = 0.88)
Our sample provided 99% power to detect an effect at the OR reported in the original study (1.31) and 84% power at the OR observed in the combined replication sample (1.18).

notes.statement: In a randomized double-blind crossover trial of 33 Parkinson disease patients homozygous for COMT Val158Met alleles (17 high-activity Val/Val and 16 low-activity Met/Met), Corvol et al. (2011) found that adding 200 mg entacapone to an acute levodopa challenge increased the best ON time more in Val/Val than in Met/Met patients (39 +/- 10 vs 9 +/- 9 minutes, p = 0.04).
quotes: Thirty-three PD patients, homozygous for the COMT alleles COMT(HH) (n = 17) and COMT(LL) (n = 16), were randomized in a double-blind crossover trial consisting of 2 successive acute levodopa challenges associated with 200mg entacapone or placebo.
The gain in the best ON time was higher in COMT(HH) than in COMT(LL) patients (39 ± 10 vs 9 ± 9 minutes, p = 0.04, interaction between treatment and genotype).

notes.statement: Corvol et al. (2011) found that, after entacapone, the levodopa area under the curve rose more in COMT Val/Val than in Met/Met PD patients (+62% vs +34%), and red blood cell COMT activity was inhibited more in Val/Val patients. They concluded that the high-activity genotype enhances the effect of entacapone on levodopa pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetics. They noted that the response after repeated doses and in heterozygotes remained to be determined.
quotes: Area under the concentration over time curve of levodopa increased more after entacapone in COMT(HH) than in COMT(LL) patients (+62 ± 6% vs +34 ± 8%, p = 0.01).
COMT inhibition by entacapone was higher in COMT(HH) than in COMT(LL) patients (-0.54 ± 0.07 vs -0.31 ± 0.06 pmol/min/mg protein, p = 0.02).
The COMT(HH) genotype in PD patients enhances the effect of entacapone on the pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetics of levodopa.

notes.statement: Alcalay et al. (2010) studied 953 patients with early-onset PD (age at onset 50 years or younger) from 13 movement disorders centers. They found mutations in 158 (16.6%): 64 (6.7%) in PRKN, 35 (3.6%) with LRRK2 G2019S, 64 (6.7%) in GBA, and 1 in DJ1. They identified no carriers of the SNCA or PINK1 mutations they tested.
quotes: One hundred fifty-eight (16.6%) participants had mutations, including 64 (6.7%) PRKN, 35 (3.6%) LRRK2 G2019S, 64 (6.7%) GBA, and 1 (0.2%) DJ1.
No carriers of the tested SNCA or PINK1 mutations were identified.

notes.statement: Alcalay et al. (2010) found mutations more often in patients with onset at age 30 or younger (40.6% vs 14.6%), in patients of Jewish ancestry (32.4% vs 13.7%), and in those with a first-degree family history of PD (23.9% vs 15.1%). Hispanic patients were more likely than non-Hispanic patients to carry PRKN mutations (15.6% vs 5.9%). The Jewish association was driven by LRRK2 G2019S and GBA N370S carriers.
quotes: Mutation carriers were more frequent in those with an AAO of 30 years or younger compared with those with AAO between 31 and 50 years (40.6% vs 14.6%, P < .001), in individuals who reported Jewish ancestry (32.4% vs 13.7%, P < .001), and in those reporting a first-degree family history of PD (23.9% vs 15.1%, P = .01).
Hispanic individuals were more likely to be PRKN carriers than non-Hispanic individuals (15.6% vs 5.9%, P = .003).
The association was driven by LRRK2 G2019S carriers and GBA N370S carriers who were more likely to be Jewish than non-Jewish (Table 4).

notes.statement: Alcalay et al. (2010) found that the GBA L444P mutation was associated with a higher UPDRS-III motor score after adjustment for covariates, and that LRRK2 G2019S carriers more often had the postural instability and gait difficulty motor phenotype. The authors cautioned that larger studies were needed to tell whether the L444P difference was a true clinical phenotype or a result of multiple comparisons.
quotes: In a linear regression model, L444P mutation status was associated with worse motor performance, as represented in a higher UPDRS-III score (OR 7.4, 95%CI 2.0–12.8, p=0.007), after adjustment for age, gender and disease duration, daily levodopa dose and history of surgical intervention for PD
Larger studies, including exams in the “off” state, are required to assess whether this statistical difference is a true clinical phenotype or a consequence of multiple comparisons.

notes.statement: Alcalay et al. (2010) concluded that patients with early-onset PD who are of Jewish or Hispanic ancestry, have onset at age 30 or younger, or have an affected first-degree relative may benefit from genetic counseling. Because penetrance of these mutations is unknown, they saw little or no role for predictive or prenatal testing.
quotes: In summary, EOPD individuals of Jewish or Hispanic ancestry, those with AAO ≤ 30, and those with a family history of PD in a first-degree relative may benefit from genetic counseling.
Therefore, there is little or no role for genetic testing for PD in family planning, predictive, or prenatal testing at this time.

notes.statement: In a genomewide association study of 2,000 PD patients and 1,986 controls from the NeuroGenetics Research Consortium (NGRC), Hamza et al. (2010) found a new association with the HLA region on chromosome 6p21.3, peaking at rs3129882 in intron 1 of HLA-DRA (P = 2.9 x 10(-8)). The association replicated in 2 datasets (meta-analysis OR 1.26, P = 1.9 x 10(-10)).
quotes: We uncovered a novel genetic association with PD in the HLA region (chromosome 6p21.3). The peak significance was at the rs3129882 polymorphism in intron 1 of HLA-DRA gene.
We replicated association of rs3129882 in two independent data sets, (Table 1, ORMeta-analysis=1.26, PMeta-analysis=1.9×10−10).

notes.statement: Hamza et al. (2010) found that the HLA association was uniform across strata of family history, age at onset, sex and environmental exposure, and was particularly strong for sporadic PD (P = 5.5 x 10(-10)), late-onset PD (P = 2.4 x 10(-8)) and men. There was no evidence of interaction with smoking, coffee, NSAIDs, SNCA or MAPT.
quotes: Associations were particularly strong for sporadic PD (P=5.5×10−10), late-onset PD (P=2.4×10−8), and men (P=1.1×10−7).
There was no evidence for gene-environment or gene-gene interaction between rs219882 and smoking (P=0.42), coffee (P=0.55), NSAIDs (P=0.65), SNCA rs356220 (P=0.78) or MAPT rs199533 (P=0.24).

notes.statement: Hamza et al. (2010) confirmed associations of PD with SNCA (P = 3.4 x 10(-11)) and MAPT (P = 1.3 x 10(-6)), and replicated an association with GAK on 4p16 (rs11248051; combined with Pankratz data, OR 1.46, P = 3.2 x 10(-9)). They did not replicate PARK16, and found only weak support for BST1 and common LRRK2 variants.
quotes: Our GWAS confirmed the known PD-susceptibility regions at SNCA (P=3.4×10−11) and MAPT (P=1.3×10−6), as we had previously reported.

We confirmed the association of PD with cyclin G-associated kinase (GAK, 4p16, Supplementary Figure 3), as suggested by Pankratz et al. (rs11248051 PNGRC=3.1×10−4, ORNGRC+Pankratz =1.46, PNGRC+Pankratz =3.2×10−9).
We did not replicate PARK16 (ORs were in opposite direction from Satake results, P=0.03–0.15).

notes.statement: Using NGRC data, Hamza et al. (2010) estimated that heritability of PD declined from 0.6 to 0.4 after excluding known pathogenic and susceptibility loci but remained significant, suggesting additional unidentified genes. Combined risk alleles at SNCA, MAPT, GAK and HLA had cumulative effects: carriers of 6 or more risk alleles had about 5-fold higher risk than those with 0 or 1 (OR 4.95).
quotes: Heritability of PD declined from 0.6 (P<0.0001) to 0.4 (P=0.01), but was still significant, suggesting additional unidentified genes exist.
was five-fold higher for individuals who had six or more risk alleles (OR=4.95, 95%CI=3.20–7.64, P=5.5×10−13).

notes.statement: Hamza et al. (2010) found significant population substructure among European Americans, correlating with Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry and European country of origin. The frequency of the rs3129882 risk allele in controls ranged from 0.36 in Washington to 0.46 in New York, and followed a gradient across Europe that was low in Northern and high in Southern Europeans, particularly Italians.
quotes: The frequency of rs3129882 risk allele varied significantly in controls (P=0.0007), from 0.36 in Washington to 0.46 in New York.
Similarly, we observed a frequency gradient across Europe, low in subjects with Northern-European ancestry and high in Southern-Europeans, particularly Italians (Supplementary Table 2).

notes.statement: Hamza et al. (2010) noted that previous eQTL analyses had identified rs3129882 as a cis-acting regulatory variant whose genotype correlated with expression of HLA-DRA, HLA-DQA2 and HLA-DRB5. They suggested that the HLA association supports a role for neuroinflammation in PD, given elevated HLA-DR expression and DR-positive reactive microglia in PD brain.
quotes: Two eQTL analyses, one using microarrays and the other RNA-seq, had identified rs3129882 as a cis-acting regulatory variation that correlated significantly (P=10−7 to 10−4) with expression levels of HLA-DRA, HLA-DQA2, and HLA-DRB5.

The evidence for genetic association with HLA, particularly when obtained from a hypothesis-free GWAS, lends strong and independent support to the involvement of neuro-inflammation and humoral immunity in PD pathogenesis.

notes.statement: Tan et al. (2010) analyzed 13 SNPs at Parkinson disease loci identified by genomewide association studies (PARK16, PARK8, PARK1, and BST1) in 2 case-control cohorts totaling 1,349 ethnic Chinese subjects. They found association with the PARK16, PARK8, and PARK1 loci but not with BST1. PARK16 SNPs were associated with decreased risk, and PARK1 and PARK8 SNPs with increased risk, of PD.
quotes: We conducted an analysis of 13 SNPs associated with PD GWAS-linked loci in 2 case-control cohorts comprised of 1,349 ethnic Chinese subjects.

PARK16, PARK8, and PARK1 loci but not BST1 were found to be associated with PD. PARK16 SNPs were associated with a decreased risk while PARK1 and PARK8 SNPs were associated with an increased risk of PD.

notes.statement: In a pooled analysis of their Chinese cohorts and 2 Japanese replication cohorts, totaling 1,366 PD patients and 16,669 controls, Tan et al. (2010) found robust association with the PARK16, PARK1, and PARK8 loci and also with BST1. The strength of association was similar in Chinese and Japanese subjects.
quotes: A pooled analysis of our Chinese cohorts and 2 Japanese replication cohorts involving 1,366 subjects with PD and 16,669 controls revealed robust association with these 3 loci and also BST1.
the strength of association is similar between Chinese and Japanese subjects

notes.statement: Tan et al. (2010) observed a trend toward a stronger protective effect of PARK16 SNPs in sporadic PD than in familial cases. The same trend was seen in older compared with younger subjects.
quotes: There was a trend toward a stronger protective effect of SNPs at the PARK16 locus in sporadic PD compared to familial cases and in older compared to younger subjects.

notes.statement: Using PET with the selective serotonin 2A receptor ligand setoperone F 18, Ballanger et al. (2010) found that 7 nondemented PD patients with visual hallucinations had higher serotonin 2A receptor binding than 7 age-matched PD patients without hallucinations. The increase was in the ventral visual pathway (bilateral inferooccipital gyrus, right fusiform gyrus, inferotemporal cortex) and in the bilateral dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, medial orbitofrontal cortex, and insula. The authors suggested that serotonin 2A receptors may help mediate visual hallucinations in PD through the ventral visual pathway.
quotes: Patients having PD with VHs demonstrate increased serotonin 2A receptor binding in the ventral visual pathway (including the bilateral inferooccipital gyrus, right fusiform gyrus, and inferotemporal cortex) as well as the bilateral dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, medial orbitofrontal cortex, and insula.
This pilot study provides the first in vivo evidence suggesting a role for serotonin 2A receptors in mediating VHs via the ventral visual pathway in PD.

notes.statement: Ballanger et al. (2010) proposed that selective serotonin 2A receptor antagonists be studied as treatment for visual hallucinations and psychosis in PD.
quotes: Treatment studies should be performed using selective serotonin 2A receptor antagonists, which have important implications for the clinical management of VHs and psychosis in PD.

notes.statement: Guella et al. (2010) found that the PDXK rs2010795 variant was not associated with Parkinson disease in an Italian population.
quotes: The PDXK rs2010795 variant is not associated with Parkinson disease in Italy.

notes.statement: Vilariño-Güell et al. (2010) reported an association between pyridoxal kinase (PDXK) and Parkinson disease.
quotes: Association of pyridoxal kinase and Parkinson disease.

notes.statement: Elstner et al. (2009) found that SNP rs2010795, in intron 8 of the PDXK gene, was associated with increased risk of PD in 676 German patients compared with German controls (p = 0.00032; OR, 1.319). The association was replicated in British (p = 0.028) and Italian (p = 0.0025) cohorts. In the combined analysis of 1,232 PD patients and 2,802 controls, p = 1.18 x 10(-7) (OR, 1.304; 95% CI, 1.178-1.444).
quotes: We identified a DNA variant (rs2010795) in PDXK associated with an increased risk of PD in the German cohort (p = 0.00032).
In the combined analysis of 1,232 PD and 2,802 control individuals, the association of SNP rs2010795 reached a p value of 1.18 × 10−7 (combined OR, 1.304; 95% CI, 1.178–1.444).

notes.statement: Elstner et al. (2009) also found that a second PDXK SNP, rs2070535 in the 3-prime untranslated region, was associated with PD in the German cohort (p = 6.4 x 10(-4); OR, 0.783). They found no association for tagging SNPs in the TRAPPC4 gene.
quotes: rs2070535 (p = 6.4 × 10−4; OR, 0.783; 95% CI, 0.681–0.901) in the 3′ untranslated region of the PDXK gene
No association was seen for tagging SNPs in the TRAPPC4 gene.

notes.statement: Elstner et al. (2009) carried out whole-genome expression profiling of laser-microdissected substantia nigra pars compacta neurons from 8 patients with PD and 9 controls. After Bonferroni correction, 4 transcripts differed significantly: MTND2, PDXK, and SRGAP3 were upregulated and TRAPPC4 was downregulated. Real-time PCR confirmed the upregulation of ND2 (2.5-fold) and PDXK (1.8-fold).
quotes: Statistical analysis of the genome-wide expression profiles using stringent Bonferroni correction revealed four transcripts to be significantly altered between PD and control samples
Upregulation of ND2 and PDXK was confirmed by real-time analysis (ND2: +2.5-fold; PDXK: +1.8-fold).

notes.statement: In dopaminergic neurons from PD patients, Elstner et al. (2009) found that mtDNA-encoded respiratory chain genes (ND1, ND2, ND4, ND5, COXII) were upregulated. In contrast, 13 nuclear genes encoding subunits of the respiratory chain were downregulated, showing inverse regulation at the single-cell level.
quotes: Interestingly, the mtDNA-encoded genes were all found to be upregulated
In contrast, the 13 nuclear genes coding for different members of the five respiratory chain complexes were robustly downregulated.

notes.statement: Elstner et al. (2009) noted that PDXK converts vitamin B6 to pyridoxal 5-prime-phosphate, a cofactor of dopa decarboxylase. They suggested that PDXK polymorphisms might affect PD risk by influencing the amount or activity of the enzyme in substantia nigra neurons.
quotes: Our data is the first to indicate an effect of polymorphisms in the PDXK gene on the risk for PD, possibly by influencing enzyme amount or activity in dopaminergic neurons of the SNc.

notes.statement: Satake et al. (2009) did a genome-wide association study and two replication studies in a total of 2,011 PD cases and 18,381 controls from Japan. They found a new susceptibility locus on 1q32 (P = 1.52 x 10(-12)), which they designated PARK16, and a second new risk locus at BST1 on 4p15 (P = 3.94 x 10(-9)).
quotes: we performed a genome-wide association study (GWAS) and two replication studies in a total of 2,011 cases and 18,381 controls from Japan
We identified a new susceptibility locus on 1q32 (P = 1.52 x 10(-12)) and designated this as PARK16, and we also identified BST1 on 4p15 as a second new risk locus (P = 3.94 x 10(-9)).

notes.statement: Satake et al. (2009) found strong associations with PD at SNCA on 4q22 (P = 7.35 x 10(-17)) and LRRK2 on 12q12 (P = 2.72 x 10(-8)) in Japanese patients. Both genes are involved in autosomal dominant forms of parkinsonism, so the authors concluded that these loci also play a part in typical PD.
quotes: We also detected strong associations at SNCA on 4q22 (P = 7.35 x 10(-17)) and LRRK2 on 12q12 (P = 2.72 x 10(-8)), both of which are implicated in autosomal dominant forms of parkinsonism.
show involvement of autosomal dominant parkinsonism loci in typical PD

notes.statement: Satake et al. (2009) compared their results with a GWAS in individuals of European ancestry. PARK16, SNCA and LRRK2 were risk loci in both populations, while BST1 and MAPT showed differences between populations. The authors suggested that population differences contribute to genetic heterogeneity in PD.
quotes: By comparing results of a GWAS performed on individuals of European ancestry, we identified PARK16, SNCA and LRRK2 as shared risk loci for PD and BST1 and MAPT as loci showing population differences.
suggest that population differences contribute to genetic heterogeneity in PD

notes.statement: Simón-Sánchez et al. (2009) ran a 2-stage genome-wide association study of Parkinson disease in people of European ancestry: 1,713 cases and 3,978 controls, then replication in 3,361 cases and 4,573 controls. They found strong association at SNCA (rs2736990, OR = 1.23, P = 2.24 x 10(-16)) and at the MAPT locus (rs393152, OR = 0.77, P = 1.95 x 10(-16)).
quotes: We performed a genome-wide association study (GWAS) in 1,713 individuals of European ancestry with Parkinson's disease (PD) and 3,978 controls. After replication in 3,361 cases and 4,573 controls, we observed two strong association signals, one in the gene encoding alpha-synuclein (SNCA; rs2736990, OR = 1.23, P = 2.24 x 10(-16)) and another at the MAPT locus (rs393152, OR = 0.77, P = 1.95 x 10(-16)).

notes.statement: Simón-Sánchez et al. (2009) replicated a locus on chromosome 1q32 that had been found in a Japanese cohort and designated it PARK16 (rs823128, OR = 0.66, combined P = 7.29 x 10(-8)). The locus spans 5 transcripts: SNORA72, NUCKS1, RAB7L1, SLC41A1, and PM20D1. They did not replicate the 4p15 signal around BST1, possibly because the associated SNPs have a low minor allele frequency in Caucasians.
quotes: We replicated the effect of a new locus detected in the Japanese cohort (PARK16, rs823128, OR = 0.66, P = 7.29 x 10(-8))
The PARK16 locus spans 5 transcripts, SNORA72, NUCKS1, RAB7L1, SLC41A1 and PM20D1.

Although we failed to replicate the signal on chromosome 4p15, which included only one gene, BST1, the low minor allele frequency of the associated SNPs in Caucasian individuals may have affected our ability to observe association.

notes.statement: Simón-Sánchez et al. (2009) found supporting evidence that common variation near LRRK2 modulates Parkinson disease risk (rs1491923, 0.17 Mb upstream of LRRK2; OR = 1.14, combined P = 1.55 x 10(-5)). The signal did not pass their multiple-testing threshold, and they could not rule out the neighboring gene SLC2A13.
quotes: provide supporting evidence that common variation around LRRK2 modulates risk for PD (rs1491923, OR = 1.14, P = 1.55 x 10(-5))
SLC2A13, neighboring LRRK2, cannot be ruled out as the gene of effect at this locus, however, LRRK2 is clearly a more plausible candidate.

notes.statement: Simón-Sánchez et al. (2009) found that most of the associated SNCA SNPs clustered in the 3-prime linkage disequilibrium block. They suggested the causal variant might affect post-transcriptional RNA processing or stability. The REP1 risk allele was in linkage disequilibrium with the 3-prime risk alleles, and its association was not independent of them.
quotes: The 3′ block contains three of the four significantly associated SNPs, suggesting that the causal variant is located in the 3′ region of the SNCA gene.

The clustering of associated SNPs in the 3′ UTR suggests that the causal variant might affect post-transcriptional RNA processing or RNA stability, possibly mediated by miRNA binding sites or by alternative splicing.
This is supported by logistic regression analysis conditioned on REP1 genotypes, showing that association at REP1 is not independent from the association identified here

notes.statement: Simón-Sánchez et al. (2009) found that the MAPT risk alleles were in linkage disequilibrium with the H1 haplotype. In 133 human frontal cortex samples, the risk alleles were associated with higher MAPT expression and lower LRRC37A expression. Risk SNPs at the SNCA, LRRK2, and PARK16 loci showed no association with expression of nearby genes.
quotes: Available genotype data of the H1/H2 haplotypes in this region showed that the risk alleles of the associated SNPs are in LD with the H1 haplotype (r2=0.761 with rs393152; supplementary figure 7B).
Notably, the allele associated with higher risk for PD, A, is associated with high levels of MAPT expression and low levels of LRRC37A expression.
but did not reveal association between risk SNPs and expression levels of proximal genes at the SNCA, LRRK2 or PARK16 loci

notes.statement: Simón-Sánchez et al. (2009) proposed population-specific genetic heterogeneity in Parkinson disease, because the MAPT association was absent in the Asian cohort while the SNCA association was replicated across populations.
quotes: Further we describe a possible population specific genetic heterogeneity in this disorder, since the association to MAPT was absent in the Asian cohort.
Association to PD at SNCA was replicated in the Japanese GWAS, confirming this as a major risk locus across populations.

notes.statement: Simón-Sánchez et al. (2009) estimated the combined population attributable risk of the identified loci at about 25%. They cautioned that this value should be interpreted with care.
quotes: The combined population attributable risk associated with the identified loci, considering the genotypic counts of those most associated SNPs in our cohort, is approximately 25% (supplemental methods).
thus these values should be interpreted with caution

notes.statement: In a multicenter study from 16 centers of 5,691 patients with Parkinson disease (780 Ashkenazi Jews) and 4,898 controls (387 Ashkenazi Jews), Sidransky et al. (2009) found a strong association between GBA mutations and PD. The Mantel-Haenszel odds ratio for any GBA mutation in patients versus controls was 5.43 across centers. The combined odds ratios were 3.96 for N370S and 6.73 for L444P.
quotes: The odds ratio for any GBA mutation in patients versus controls was 5.43 across centers.
This allows for confidence in reporting the Mantel-Haenszel combined ORs attributable to N370S (OR = 3.96, 95% CI 2.6–6.02) and L444P (OR = 6.73, 95% CI 4.5–15.42).

notes.statement: Sidransky et al. (2009) found N370S or L444P in 15.3% of Ashkenazi Jewish PD patients versus 3.4% of controls, and in 3.2% of non-Ashkenazi patients versus 0.6% of controls. N370S was not seen in any Asian patients or controls. When GBA was fully sequenced in non-Ashkenazi patients, 6.9% carried a mutation.
quotes: one of these two mutations were found in 15.3% of Ashkenazi Jewish patients versus 3.4% of controls, and in 3.2% of non-Ashkenazi patients versus 0.6% of controls.
N370S was particularly prevalent among Ashkenazi Jews (OR 5.62, 95%CL 3.04–10.39) and was not seen among any of the Asian patients or controls

notes.statement: Sidransky et al. (2009) concluded that all GBA exons need to be sequenced. Among non-Ashkenazi cases, as many as 46% of mutant alleles could be missed when screening for only N370S and L444P. In addition, 22 of 43 subjects with L444P carried recombinant alleles that included pseudogene sequence.
quotes: Our data demonstrate that among non-Ashkenazi cases as many as 46% of mutant alleles can be missed when screening for only two mutations.
Moreover, 22 of 43 subjects with L444P carried other pseudogene sequence and hence had recombinant alleles.

notes.statement: Sidransky et al. (2009) found that, compared with noncarriers, PD patients with GBA mutations presented about 4 years earlier and were more likely to have an affected relative. Carriers less often had asymmetric onset, bradykinesia, rest tremor and rigidity. Cognitive changes were reported more often in carriers (26.3% vs 19.0%).
quotes: mutations were associated with a significantly lower frequency of asymmetric onset (p-value<0.0001), bradykinesia (p-value=0.0001), resting tremor (p-value=0.0298), and rigidity (p-value<0.0001).
The presence or absence of cognitive changes was recorded for 1948 patients, reported as present in 26.3% of patients with mutations and 19.0% without (p-value= 0.0071).

notes.statement: Sidransky et al. (2009) found that the common GBA variants E326K and T369M, which are not pathogenic in Gaucher disease, were not significantly associated with Parkinson disease.
quotes: Full sequencing data identified two common GBA variants, E326K and T369M which are not pathogenic in subjects with Gaucher disease. Neither demonstrated a significant association with Parkinson disease.

notes.statement: Sidransky et al. (2009) concluded that GBA mutations are likely a susceptibility factor rather than a mendelian cause of Parkinson disease. They added that GBA mutations are among the most common risk factors for PD identified to date.
quotes: While mutations in GBA are likely to be a susceptibility factor rather than a Mendelian cause of Parkinson disease, the high frequency of mutations among ethnically diverse heterogeneous cohorts of subjects with Parkinson disease render mutations in this gene among the most common and universally found risk factors

notes.statement: In a prospective study of 157,036 men and women without PD at baseline in 2 US cohorts (Health Professionals Follow-up Study and Nurses' Health Study), Gao et al. (2009) identified 616 incident PD cases over 14 to 20 years of follow-up. A family history of melanoma in a first-degree relative was associated with a higher risk of PD (multivariate relative risk 1.85; 95% CI 1.2-2.8; p = 0.004) after adjustment for smoking, ethnicity, caffeine intake, and other covariates.
quotes: During 14-20 years follow-up, we identified 616 incident PD cases. A family history of melanoma in a first-degree relative was associated with a higher risk of PD (multivariate relative risk = 1.85; 95% confidence interval: 1.2, 2.8; p = 0.004), after adjusting for smoking, ethnicity, caffeine intake, and other covariates.

notes.statement: Gao et al. (2009) found no significant association between PD risk and a family history of colorectal, lung, prostate, or breast cancer. Interactions between melanoma family history and age, smoking, or caffeine intake were not significant.
quotes: In contrast, we did not observe significant associations between a family history of colorectal, lung, prostate, or breast cancer and PD risk.
Interactions between melanoma family history and age, smoking, or caffeine intake were not significant and subgroup analyses according to these factors generated similar results.

notes.statement: Gao et al. (2009) concluded that their findings supported the notion that melanoma and PD share common genetic components, and suggested that the genetic determinants of melanoma could be explored as susceptibility candidate genes for PD.
quotes: Our findings support the notion that melanoma and Parkinson disease (PD) share common genetic components. The genetic determinants of melanoma could therefore be explored as susceptibility candidate genes for PD.

notes.statement: Plaitakis et al. (2010) found that a rare T1492G variant in the X-linked GLUD2 gene, which causes a Ser445Ala substitution in the regulatory domain of hGDH2, interacted significantly with age at onset of PD in Caucasian populations. Hemizygous carriers developed PD 6 to 13 years earlier than subjects with other genotypes in two independent Greek PD groups and one North American PD cohort.
quotes: we report that a rare T1492G variant in GLUD2, an X-linked gene encoding a glutamate dehydrogenase (a mitochondrial enzyme central to glutamate metabolism) that is expressed in brain (hGDH2), interacted significantly with age at PD onset in Caucasian populations.

Individuals hemizygous for this GLUD2 coding change that results in substitution of Ala for Ser445 in the regulatory domain of hGDH2 developed PD 6-13 years earlier than did subjects with other genotypes

notes.statement: Plaitakis et al. (2010) found no effect on age at onset in female PD patients who were heterozygous for the GLUD2 Ser445Ala variant. They suggested that this lack of effect could be related to modification of the overactive variant enzyme by estrogens.
quotes: However, this effect was not present in female PD patients who were heterozygous for the DNA change.
The lack of effect in female heterozygous PD patients could be related to a modification of the overactive variant enzyme by estrogens.

notes.statement: Plaitakis et al. (2010) found that the Ser445Ala variant hGDH2 enzyme had enhanced basal activity that resisted GTP inhibition but was markedly sensitive to modification by estrogens. They concluded that this gain-of-function rare polymorphism hastens PD onset in hemizygous subjects, probably by damaging nigral cells through enhanced glutamate oxidative dehydrogenation.
quotes: The variant enzyme, obtained by substitution of Ala for Ser445, showed an enhanced basal activity that was resistant to GTP inhibition but markedly sensitive to modification by estrogens.
Thus, a gain-of-function rare polymorphism in hGDH2 hastens the onset of PD in hemizygous subjects, probably by damaging nigral cells through enhanced glutamate oxidative dehydrogenation.

notes.statement: Lees et al. (2009) described Parkinson disease as a common progressive bradykinetic disorder that can be accurately diagnosed. It is characterized by severe loss of nigral cells in the pars compacta and by aggregated alpha-synuclein that builds up in specific brainstem, spinal cord and cortical regions.
quotes: Parkinson's disease is a common progressive bradykinetic disorder that can be accurately diagnosed. It is characterised by the presence of severe pars-compacta nigral-cell loss, and accumulation of aggregated alpha-synuclein in specific brain stem, spinal cord, and cortical regions.

notes.statement: Lees et al. (2009) noted that age is the main known risk factor for Parkinson disease. They added that susceptibility genes, including alpha-synuclein, LRRK2 and GBA, have shown that genetic predisposition is another important causal factor.
quotes: The main known risk factor is age. Susceptibility genes including alpha-synuclein, leucine rich repeat kinase 2 (LRRK-2), and glucocerebrosidase (GBA) have shown that genetic predisposition is another important causal factor.

notes.statement: Lees et al. (2009) stated that dopamine replacement therapy considerably reduces motor handicap in Parkinson disease. Treating the associated depression, pain, constipation and nocturnal difficulties can improve quality of life. They described embryonic stem cells and gene therapy as promising approaches still at the research stage.
quotes: Dopamine replacement therapy considerably reduces motor handicap, and effective treatment of associated depression, pain, constipation, and nocturnal difficulties can improve quality of life. Embryonic stem cells and gene therapy are promising research therapeutic approaches.

notes.statement: Gan-Or et al. (2009) reported that Parkinson disease patients carrying severe GBA mutations differed in phenotype from those carrying mild GBA mutations.
quotes: Differential phenotype in Parkinson's disease patients with severe versus mild GBA mutations.

notes.statement: In 600 Ashkenazi PD patients, Gan-Or et al. (2010) found that, compared with non-carriers, more LRRK2 G2019S carriers reported rigidity (p = 0.007) and balance disturbances (p = 0.008) as their initial symptoms, whereas more GBA mutation carriers reported bradykinesia (p = 0.021). The authors suggested that LRRK2 and GBA mutations have distinct effects on the initial symptoms of PD.
quotes: Reported initial symptoms were compared between three genotypic groups of patients: carriers of GBA mutations, carriers of LRRK2 G2019S mutation, and non-carriers.
More LRRK2 G2019S carriers reported muscle stiffness (rigidity, p = 0.007) and balance disturbances (p = 0.008), while more GBA mutation carriers reported slowness (bradykinesia, p = 0.021).
These results suggest distinct effects of LRRK2 or GBA mutations on the initial symptoms of PD.

notes.statement: Gao et al. (2009) ran a genome-wide linkage screen of 5,824 SNPs in 278 families of European, non-Hispanic descent with PD. They used parametric and nonparametric analyses that allowed for genetic heterogeneity. They found significant evidence for linkage on chromosome 18q11 (maximum lod score = 4.1) and suggestive evidence for linkage on chromosome 3q25 (maximum lod score = 2.5).
quotes: We conducted a genome-wide linkage screen of 5824 single-nucleotide polymorphisms in 278 families of European, non-Hispanic descent to localize regions that harbor susceptibility loci for PD.
Significant evidence for linkage was detected on chromosome 18q11 (maximum lod score [MLOD] = 4.1) and suggestive evidence for linkage was obtained on chromosome 3q25 (MLOD = 2.5).

notes.statement: Gao et al. (2009) found that the linkage results were strongest in families that had not previously been screened for linkage. Simulation studies suggested that the findings were likely due to locus heterogeneity rather than random statistical error.
quotes: These results were strongest in families not previously screened for linkage, and simulation studies suggest that these findings are likely due to locus heterogeneity rather than random statistical error.

notes.statement: Neumann et al. (2009) screened GBA in 790 British patients with Parkinson disease and 257 controls matched for age and ethnicity. GBA mutations were found in 33 of 790 patients (4.18%) and 3 of 257 controls (1.17%) (p = 0.01; OR 3.7; 95% CI 1.12-12.14). Fourteen different mutations were found, 3 of them novel.
quotes: We utilized the DNA of 790 patients and 257 controls, matched for age and ethnicity, to screen for mutations within the GBA gene.

The frequency of GBA mutations among the British patients (33/790 = 4.18%) was significantly higher (P = 0.01; odds ratio = 3.7; 95% confidence interval = 1.12-12.14) when compared to the control group (3/257 = 1.17%).

notes.statement: Neumann et al. (2009) found widespread, abundant alpha-synuclein pathology in all 17 GBA mutation carriers examined, graded Braak stage 5-6. Diffuse neocortical Lewy body-type pathology tended to occur more often in GBA carriers than in matched Parkinson disease controls without GBA mutations.
quotes: Pathological examination revealed widespread and abundant alpha-synuclein pathology in all 17 GBA mutation carriers, which were graded as Braak stage of 5-6
Diffuse neocortical Lewy body-type pathology tended to occur more frequently in the group with GBA mutations compared to matched Parkinson's disease controls.

notes.statement: Neumann et al. (2009) concluded that GBA mutations occur in British Parkinson disease patients at a higher frequency than mutations in any other known Parkinson disease gene. They suggested that GBA mutations are a significant risk factor and, to date, the most common genetic factor identified for the disease.
quotes: This study demonstrates that GBA mutations are found in British subjects at a higher frequency than any other known Parkinson's disease gene.
suggest that to date, this is the most common genetic factor identified for the disease.

notes.statement: In the Health Professionals Follow-up Study and the Nurses' Health Study, Gao et al. (2009) followed 38,641 men and 93,661 women who did not have PD at baseline. PD risk rose as natural hair color became lighter. After adjustment for age, smoking, ethnicity and other covariates, the pooled relative risks were 1.0, 1.40, 1.61, and 1.93 (95% CI, 1.08-3.43) for black, brown, blond, and red hair, respectively.
quotes: We included 38,641 men and 93,661 women who were free of PD at baseline.

Pooled RRs for PD were 1 (reference), 1.40, 1.61, and 1.93 (95% confidence interval, 1.1-3.4) for black, brown, blond, and red hair, respectively, after adjusting for age, smoking, ethnicity, and other covariates.

notes.statement: Gao et al. (2009) found that the association between hair color and PD was strongest for onset before age 70 years (adjusted RR for red vs black hair, 3.83; 95% CI, 1.7-8.7). Hair color was not significantly associated with PD that began at age 70 or older.
quotes: The associations between hair color and PD were particularly strong for relative younger onset of PD (<70 yr) (adjusted RR for red vs black hair = 3.83; 95% confidence interval, 1.7-8.7).
In contrast, hair color was not significantly associated with risk of PD onset at 70+ years.

notes.statement: Gao et al. (2009) genotyped the MC1R Arg151Cys polymorphism in a case-control study nested in the two cohorts (272 cases and 1,185 controls successfully genotyped). Compared with Arg/Arg, the Cys/Cys genotype, which was associated with red hair, carried a higher PD risk (adjusted RR, 3.15; 95% CI, 1.06-9.37). Participants with red hair who were Cys/Cys homozygotes had a relative risk of 4.9 (95% CI, 1.5-16.2).
quotes: Of these, 272 cases and 1185 controls were successful genotyped and included in the current analyses.
The Cys/Cys genotype was associated with a higher PD risk, relative to the Arg/Arg genotype (adjusted RR=3.15; 95% CI: 1.06, 9.37) (Table 3).

Participants with red hair plus carrying Cys/Cys variant were more than four times (RR=4.9, 95% CI: 1.5, 16.2) more likely to have PD relative to those who did not have red hair and did not carry the Cys allele (Table 3).

notes.statement: Gao et al. (2009) suggested that pigmentation may play a role in PD. They proposed that this might partly explain why PD and melanoma occur together more often than expected, rather than the association being an adverse effect of levodopa.
quotes: Our findings suggest that the higher frequency of melanoma occurring among individuals with PD may be at least in part explained by the associations of both diseases with a lighter hair color and the MC1R Arg151Cys variant allele, rather than being an adverse effect of levodopa treatment as previously suggested.

notes.statement: Pankratz et al. (2009) performed a genomewide association study in 857 familial PD cases negative for the LRRK2 G2019S mutation and 867 controls using the Illumina HumanCNV370Duo array. No result met genomewide significance; the strongest association was with SNPs in the GAK/DGKQ region on chromosome 4p (additive model p = 3.4 x 10(-6); OR = 1.69).
quotes: Genotyping was performed with the Illumina HumanCNV370Duo array in 857 familial PD cases and 867 controls.

No result met genomewide significance based on a conservative Bonferroni correction. The strongest association result was with SNPs in the GAK/DGKQ region on chromosome 4 (additive model: p = 3.4 x 10(-6); OR = 1.69).

notes.statement: Pankratz et al. (2009) found consistent evidence of association with the chromosomal regions containing SNCA (additive model p = 5.5 x 10(-5); OR = 1.35, rs356229) and MAPT (recessive model p = 2.0 x 10(-5); OR = 0.56), neither of which had been identified in previous PD GWAS.
quotes: Consistent evidence of association was also observed to the chromosomal regions containing SNCA (additive model: p = 5.5 x 10(-5); OR = 1.35) and MAPT (recessive model: p = 2.0 x 10(-5); OR = 0.56).
The rs356229 SNP that we report with a minor allele increasing risk of PD (OR = 1.35) exhibits modest LD with rs356219 (HapMap CEPH D′ = 0.65, r2 = 0.39).

notes.statement: In a meta-analysis combining their data with the case-control GWAS of Fung et al., Pankratz et al. (2009) obtained improved p values for the GAK/DGKQ region (additive model p = 2.5 x 10(-7)) and the MAPT region (recessive p = 9.8 x 10(-6); additive p = 4.8 x 10(-5)), as well as for PIK3CD, FIGN, and LY75/PLA2R1, suggesting new susceptibility alleles for PD in the GAK/DGKQ region.
quotes: Meta-analysis was performed using data from a previous case-control GWAS, and yielded improved p values for several regions, including GAK/DGKQ (additive model: p = 2.5 x 10(-7)) and the MAPT region (recessive model: p = 9.8 x 10(-6); additive model: p = 4.8 x 10(-5)).
These included the C17orf69/MAPT region, PIK3CD, LOC643954/HS3ST5 and FIGN (Table 3).

notes.statement: Pankratz et al. (2009) noted that GAK, encoding cyclin G-associated kinase, was a promising candidate because it had been shown to be differentially expressed (1.56-fold) in the substantia nigra pars compacta of PD patients compared to controls; minor alleles of SNPs tagging the MAPT H2 haplotype were associated with reduced risk in the additive meta-analysis.
quotes: GAK is a particularly promising candidate because it is one of 137 genes shown to be differentially expressed in PD, with a 1.56-fold change in expression in the substantia nigra pars compacta of PD patients as compared to controls.

Minor alleles of SNPs genotyped in this study that tag the H2 haplotype include rs12185268/G, rs12373139/A, rs1981997/A, and rs8070723/G, all of which were highlighted in the results of the additive meta-analysis (Table 4).

notes.statement: Gutti et al. (2008) stressed that cohorts with Parkinson disease need appropriate genotyping strategies to detect glucocerebrosidase (GBA) mutations.
quotes: The need for appropriate genotyping strategies for glucocerebrosidase mutations in cohorts with Parkinson disease.

notes.statement: Gan-Or et al. (2008) screened 420 Israeli Ashkenazi Jewish patients with PD, 333 elderly controls, and 3,805 young controls for 8 GBA mutations. GBA carrier frequency was 17.9% in patients compared to 4.2% in elderly and 6.35% in young controls, and more than one-third of the patients carried a mutation in GBA or LRRK2.
quotes: GBA carrier frequency was 17.9% in patients with PD compared to 4.2% in elderly and 6.35% in young controls.
a surprisingly high frequency, more than one third of our patient population, carried a mutation in GBA or LRRK2.

notes.statement: Gan-Or et al. (2008) found that GBA mutations associated with severe Gaucher disease (84GG, IVS2+1, V394L, D409H, L444P, RecTL) increased PD risk 13.6-fold, while mild mutations (N370S, R496H) increased it 2.2-fold. Severe and mild mutation carriers had mean ages at onset of 55.7 and 57.9 years, compared with 60.7 years in patients without known GBA or LRRK2 mutations. Severe mutations made up 29% of GBA carriers among patients versus 7% among young controls.
quotes: The proportion of severe mutation carriers among PD patient GBA carriers was 29% compared to 7% among young controls.

Severe and mild GBA mutations increased the risk of developing PD by 13.6- and 2.2-fold, and affected the average age at PD onset (AAO), 55.7 and 57.9 years, compared to 60.7 years in patients without known GBA or LRRK2 mutations.

notes.statement: Gan-Or et al. (2008) observed an earlier age at onset in Ashkenazi PD patients who carried LRRK2 G2019S.
quotes: Additionally, an earlier AAO was observed in LRRK2 G2019S carrier PD patients.

notes.statement: In a case-control study of 721 patients with PD, 57 patients with dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB), and 554 controls from 4 movement disorder clinics in the Seattle area, Mata et al. (2008) screened for the 2 most common GBA mutations, N370S and L444P. Heterozygote frequency was significantly higher in patients with PD (2.9%; P less than 0.001) and DLB (3.5%; P = 0.045) than in controls (0.4%).
quotes: Seven hundred twenty-one patients with PD, 554 healthy control subjects, and 57 patients with DLB.
We observed a significantly higher heterozygote frequency for the 2 mutations in patients with PD (2.9%; P <.001) and those with DLB (3.5%; P = .045) compared with control subjects (0.4%).

notes.statement: Mata et al. (2008) concluded that GBA mutations had a large effect on susceptibility to Lewy body disorders at the individual level, but a modest population-attributable risk of approximately 3% in individuals of European ancestry.
quotes: Our findings suggest that GBA mutations exert a large effect on susceptibility for Lewy body disorders at the individual level but are associated with a modest (approximately 3%) population-attributable risk in individuals of European ancestry.

notes.statement: In a case-control study of 418 PD patients and 468 race-, sex- and age-matched controls, Tan et al. (2007) found a significant inverse association between caffeine intake and PD (P = 2.01 x 10(-5)). Compared with low drinkers, the odds ratio was 0.71 (95% CI 0.50-1.00) for moderate drinkers and 0.47 (95% CI 0.34-0.65) for high drinkers.
quotes: 886 consisting of 418 PD and 468 race, sex and age matched controls were included.

A significant association was seen between caffeine intake and the onset of PD (P=2.01x10(-5)), with the odds ratio for moderate and high drinkers at 0.71 [95% confidence interval (CI): 0.50-1.00] and 0.47 (95% CI: 0.34-0.65), respectively against the low drinkers.

notes.statement: Tan et al. (2007) found no evidence of an association between the CYP1A2 -163C>A polymorphism (rs762551), which is associated with high CYP1A2 inducibility, and PD (P = 0.08). Multivariate analysis showed no interaction between caffeine and CYP1A2 genotype (P = 0.956). The authors concluded that the protective association with caffeine was seen in both fast and slow caffeine metabolizers, which supports experimental evidence that both caffeine and its major metabolite paraxanthine are neuroprotective.
quotes: A polymorphic variant of CYP1A2 (-163C>A) (rs762551) is associated with high CYP1A2 inducibility.
No evidence existed to suggest any association between CYP1A2 and the onset of PD (P=0.08).
Multivariate analysis revealed no evidence of any interaction effects of caffeine with CYP1A2 (P=0.956).

notes.statement: Tan et al. (2007) studied glucocerebrosidase (GBA) mutations and the risk of Parkinson disease in Chinese patients.
quotes: Glucocerebrosidase mutations and risk of Parkinson disease in Chinese patients.

notes.statement: Outeiro et al. (2007) identified a potent inhibitor of sirtuin 2 (SIRT2) and found that inhibiting SIRT2 rescued alpha-synuclein toxicity and changed the shape of inclusions in a cellular model of Parkinson disease. Knocking down SIRT2 with siRNA also rescued alpha-synuclein toxicity. The authors suggested that the results link neurodegeneration and aging.
quotes: We identified a potent inhibitor of sirtuin 2 (SIRT2) and found that inhibition of SIRT2 rescued alpha-synuclein toxicity and modified inclusion morphology in a cellular model of Parkinson's disease.
Genetic inhibition of SIRT2 via small interfering RNA similarly rescued alpha-synuclein toxicity.
The results suggest a link between neurodegeneration and aging.

notes.statement: Outeiro et al. (2007) found that SIRT2 inhibitors protected against dopaminergic cell death both in vitro and in a Drosophila model of Parkinson disease.
quotes: Furthermore, the inhibitors protected against dopaminergic cell death both in vitro and in a Drosophila model of Parkinson's disease.

notes.statement: Chan et al. (2007) suggested that substantia nigra pars compacta dopaminergic neurons are vulnerable in Parkinson disease because of their unusual reliance on L-type Cav1.3 calcium channels to drive maintained, rhythmic pacemaking, which renders them vulnerable to stressors thought to contribute to disease progression. This reliance increased with age, as juvenile neurons used pacemaking mechanisms common to neurons not affected in PD.
quotes: Our studies suggest that the unusual reliance of these neurons on L-type Ca(v)1.3 Ca2+ channels to drive their maintained, rhythmic pacemaking renders them vulnerable to stressors thought to contribute to disease progression.

The reliance on these channels increases with age, as juvenile dopamine-containing neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta use pacemaking mechanisms common to neurons not affected in Parkinson's disease.

notes.statement: Chan et al. (2007) found that blocking Cav1.3 channels in adult mouse SNc dopaminergic neurons induced reversion to the latent juvenile form of pacemaking, and that this 'rejuvenation' protected the neurons in both in vitro and in vivo models of Parkinson disease, pointing to a strategy that could slow or stop disease progression.
quotes: These mechanisms remain latent in adulthood, and blocking Ca(v)1.3 Ca2+ channels in adult neurons induces a reversion to the juvenile form of pacemaking.
Such blocking ('rejuvenation') protects these neurons in both in vitro and in vivo models of Parkinson's disease, pointing to a new strategy that could slow or stop the progression of the disease.

notes.statement: In a cross-sectional survey, Ferreira et al. (2007) found neoplastic or preneoplastic skin lesions in 35 of 150 PD patients (23.3%), compared with 20 of 146 age-matched controls (13.7%) (OR 1.92).
